# UI/UX design: research methods — facts

> Source-anchored units about UI/UX design: research methods: 170 across 36 sources. Each line ends in the URL and anchor it came from; `keywords:` names the lexicon terms that matched.

## Definitions

- [statement] User needs are one framing input alongside organizational and wider-system constraints. GOV.UK includes policy intent and operational constraints; Joffres argues that good design moves between user, strategic, planetary and societal needs. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/how-the-discovery-phase-works · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Human-centered design lifecycle and problem framing · also: https://marvelapp.com/blog/design-thinking-isnt-the-problem-human-centered-design/
- [statement] SUS is an overall post-test perceived-usability questionnaire; SEQ is a post-task rating of the difficulty of the task just attempted. Choose the instrument according to the level of experience being evaluated. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/measuring-perceived-usability/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX measurement, usability metrics and psychometric scales · also: https://measuringu.com/papers/Sauro_Dumas_CHI2009.pdf
- [statement] Treat method maps as adaptable guidance: classifications are not rigid, and research questions, organizational resources, and stakeholder needs shape the approach. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/which-ux-research-methods/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX research strategy and method selection · also: https://www.userinterviews.com/ux-research-field-guide-chapter/how-to-choose-a-research-method

## Structure and components

- [statement] GOV.UK recommends turning research questions into ordered interview topics, starter questions, and possible follow-ups; pilot the structure with a colleague and revise unclear questions or awkward flow before creating the discussion guide. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-in-depth-interviews · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/critical-incident-technique/
- [statement] A tree test isolates category structure and text labels from visual layout and other contextual cues. Its results do not by themselves establish findability in the fully designed site, where design and search can change behavior. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/card-sorting-tree-testing-differences/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Information architecture, card sorting and tree testing · also: https://measuringu.com/tree-testing-ia/, https://raw.studio/blog/card-sorting-and-tree-testing, https://www.nngroup.com/articles/interpreting-tree-test-results/
- [statement] Card-sort groupings and participant-created names are design inputs, not a ready-made navigation structure: researchers must interpret them and evaluate candidate hierarchies. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/card-sorting-tree-testing-differences/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Information architecture, card sorting and tree testing · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/card-sorting-definition/, https://www.uxmatters.com/mt/archives/2007/09/card-sorting-mistakes-made-and-lessons-learned.php
- [statement] SUS contains 10 items with five response options. Its transformed score ranges from 0 to 100 and is not a percentage or a percentile rank. (medium confidence) — https://measuringu.com/sus/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX measurement, usability metrics and psychometric scales · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/measuring-perceived-usability/

## How it works

- [statement] Balance clarification against interference: silent observation preserves more of the activity’s natural flow but can leave its meaning unclear; occasional questions add understanding, while step-by-step explanation changes how people perform the activity. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/contextual-research-and-observation · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/
- [statement] Observation may miss rare events because its time window is limited; a critical-incident interview can elicit unusual events outside that window, with the memory and typicality limitations stated above. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/critical-incident-technique/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX
- [statement] NN/G recommends explicitly transitioning from the introductory interview to watching actual work; agree that the participant can defer interruptions and redirect summaries or grievance lists back to normal work when needed. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX
- [statement] Ask for clarification when an observed action is unclear and let participants correct interpretations; reserve final questions for the end so understanding can improve without repeatedly interrupting work. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/contextual-research-and-observation · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/
- [statement] A process diagram alone is insufficient preparation for complex framing work. Joffres calls design processes scaffolding and emphasizes practitioner abilities; van der Bijl-Brouwer concludes that framing complex societal problems requires a sophisticated skillset and expertise. (medium confidence) — https://marvelapp.com/blog/design-thinking-isnt-the-problem-human-centered-design/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Human-centered design lifecycle and problem framing · also: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405872618301114
- [statement] NN/G cautions that predefined categories in hybrid sorts can bias participants toward similarly structured categories; it prefers tree testing over closed sorting when the goal is evaluating navigation categories. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/card-sorting-definition/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Information architecture, card sorting and tree testing
- [statement] Practitioner experience warns against treating every findability problem as a taxonomy problem: navigation controls and search quality may need attention even when card sorting is available. (medium confidence) — https://www.uxmatters.com/mt/archives/2007/09/card-sorting-mistakes-made-and-lessons-learned.php · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Information architecture, card sorting and tree testing · also: https://measuringu.com/tree-testing-ia/
- [statement] Pilot the tasks and instructions before launch. Unmoderated instructions must stand alone because no facilitator is present to clarify misunderstandings during the session. (high confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-moderated-usability-testing · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Moderated and unmoderated usability testing · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/remote-usability-tests/
- [statement] Unmoderated prototypes need enough scenario context to make the task understandable without an interview. David Hamill warns about missing backstory; Elise Nguyen separately reports needing more prototype context when she could not interview participants directly. (medium confidence) — https://david-hamill.medium.com/unmoderated-usability-testing-some-mistakes-to-avoid-8f2d1a3d5732 · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Moderated and unmoderated usability testing · also: https://elisenguyen.com/work/mongodb-billing
- [statement] Recruit participants who match the target users. Plan accessibility support, and let assistive-technology users use their own devices where feasible because personal configurations can be hard to replicate. (high confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-moderated-usability-testing · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Moderated and unmoderated usability testing · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/usability-testing-101/
- [statement] Choose moderated sessions when clarification and probing are important; unmoderated remote sessions suit focused tasks and flexible parallel scheduling, but lack live action-specific follow-up and may yield unusable sessions if participants misunderstand tasks or encounter technical trouble. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/remote-usability-tests/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Moderated and unmoderated usability testing
- [statement] Do not force substantially different observed journeys into one map. GOV.UK recommends a consolidated map when participants share stages and similar steps, and separate maps when groups have significantly different stages and steps. (low confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/creating-an-experience-map · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Service design, journey mapping and service blueprints
- [statement] Frog recommends testing a proposed service through prototypes before implementation so that risky assumptions encounter real users and real-world conditions. (low confidence) — https://www.frog.co/designmind/intentional-healthcare-delivery-with-service-design · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Service design, journey mapping and service blueprints
- [statement] A diagram should support investigation and change: blueprint dependencies can expose service weaknesses and redundant work. Nielsen Norman Group recommends prototyping future process changes before implementation and tracking changes against service goals. These are recommended uses, not proof that producing a diagram alone improves outcomes. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/service-blueprints-definition/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Service design, journey mapping and service blueprints · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/service-blueprinting-faq/
- [statement] SEQ asks about perceived task difficulty immediately after each task, whereas SUS concerns the overall session; use the task-level question to compare tasks, keeping tasks comparable when benchmarking. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/measuring-perceived-usability/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX measurement, usability metrics and psychometric scales · also: https://measuringu.com/papers/Sauro_Dumas_CHI2009.pdf
- [statement] UMUX-LITE uses two positively worded items about capabilities meeting requirements and ease of use. Its original researchers reported concurrent validity with SUS in two surveys and proposed it as a shorter alternative when a longer questionnaire is undesirable. (medium confidence) — https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2470654.2481287 · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX measurement, usability metrics and psychometric scales · also: https://measuringu.com/umux-lite/
- [statement] Treat validation as evidence for a particular instrument and context. The Greek UMUX-LITE study found good reliability and concurrent validity on the websites it studied, while explicitly limiting generalization because it tested only two systems of the same type. (low confidence) — https://dl.acm.org/doi/fullHtml/10.1145/3635059.3635075 · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX measurement, usability metrics and psychometric scales
- [statement] UMUX-Lite asks whether the system’s capabilities meet the respondent’s requirements and whether the system is easy to use. Its two positive items cover perceived usefulness and ease of use; it is a shorter alternative when questionnaire burden matters. (low confidence) — https://measuringu.com/umux-lite/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX measurement, usability metrics and psychometric scales
- [statement] Satisfaction scores do not explain the cause of a usability problem. Combine questionnaire scores with observed performance and follow-up investigation before deciding what design change to make. (medium confidence) — https://measuringu.com/sus/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX measurement, usability metrics and psychometric scales · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/measuring-perceived-usability/
- [statement] NN/g recommends considering context of product use when choosing a method: natural use prioritizes realism but offers less control over topics, while scripted use focuses the study on selected product areas. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/which-ux-research-methods/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX research strategy and method selection
- [statement] Plan inclusive recruitment, access needs, and informed consent explicitly; GOV.UK recommends including varied users, disabled users, and people who need support when the service has a broad audience. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/plan-user-research-for-your-service · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX research strategy and method selection · also: https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/plan-round-of-user-research
- [statement] Triangulation can add time and can encourage confirmation bias when researchers select supporting data and ignore disconfirming evidence. Dscout recommends beginning triangulation before conclusions harden or involving a partner to check bias. (low confidence) — https://dscout.com/people-nerds/triangulate-user-research · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX research strategy and method selection
- [statement] Do not use recurrence alone to discard potentially important minority cases: Anderson-Stanier explicitly notes that one-off insights can be compelling, and NN/G asks researchers to examine outliers and differences between participant groups when findings conflict. (medium confidence) — https://dscout.com/people-nerds/user-research-synthesis · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX research synthesis, personas and jobs-to-be-done · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/interpreting-research-findings/
- [statement] When evidence contradicts a theme, check how the studies were conducted before explaining away the difference. NN/g recommends examining participants, tasks, logistics and analysis, and warns against automatically overruling qualitative findings with quantitative results. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/interpreting-research-findings/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX research synthesis, personas and jobs-to-be-done
- [statement] Jobs-to-be-done frames the outcome a user seeks through a product. A job description can include circumstances and functional, emotional and social success criteria. Klement emphasizes situational motivations and anxieties when translating jobs into design work. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/personas-jobs-be-done/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX research synthesis, personas and jobs-to-be-done · also: https://www.intercom.com/blog/using-job-stories-design-features-ui-ux
- [statement] Do not assume a one-to-one relationship between personas and jobs. NN/g notes that different user groups can have different requirements for the same job, while one persona can have different jobs in different contexts. Preserve these distinctions when turning themes into needs. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/personas-jobs-be-done/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX research synthesis, personas and jobs-to-be-done

## How-to and procedures

- [statement] Use task paths to decide whether to rename, regroup, or provide multiple routes to content. ONRR’s tree test exposed competing category expectations and led the team to propose cross-listing resources and reorganizing categories. (low confidence) — https://digital.gov/2022/01/06/open-source-information-architecture-design-using-the-tools-you-have-to-conduct-card-sorting-and-tree-testing · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Information architecture, card sorting and tree testing
- [statement] Prefer moderation when understanding an unexpected action requires clarification or follow-up. Unmoderated remote studies suit focused questions with self-contained tasks and can run on participants’ own schedules. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/remote-usability-tests/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Moderated and unmoderated usability testing · also: https://github.com/sourcegraph/handbook/blob/main/content/departments/product/design/research/usability-testing-how-to.md
- [statement] Use personas to express behavior, needs, goals and relevant context. Use jobs-to-be-done to express the outcome sought and the situation and motivations behind it; demographic attributes alone do not explain the job. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/personas-jobs-be-done/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX research synthesis, personas and jobs-to-be-done · also: https://www.intercom.com/blog/using-job-stories-design-features-ui-ux

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] If work cannot safely be interrupted, observe with minimal interference and defer clarification questions until an appropriate stopping point or after the session. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://dscout.com/people-nerds/behind-scenes-contextual-inquiry
- [statement] Define the accepted destinations for each tree-test task before interpreting success. Success counts participants who select a correct final location; visiting it and then choosing another location is failure. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/tree-testing/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Information architecture, card sorting and tree testing · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/interpreting-tree-test-results/
- [statement] In ONRR’s card-sort case, a small sample spread across two audiences left some cards without a strong placement pattern; this is a case-specific sample limitation, not a universal participant threshold. (low confidence) — https://digital.gov/2022/01/06/open-source-information-architecture-design-using-the-tools-you-have-to-conduct-card-sorting-and-tree-testing · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Information architecture, card sorting and tree testing
- [statement] Limit task-learning effects: ONRR observed participants learning tree categories quickly and emphasized fewer tasks and randomized order; NN/G recommends assigning each participant only one tree version when comparing trees. (medium confidence) — https://digital.gov/2022/01/06/open-source-information-architecture-design-using-the-tools-you-have-to-conduct-card-sorting-and-tree-testing · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Information architecture, card sorting and tree testing · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/tree-testing/
- [statement] Think-aloud asks participants to verbalize thoughts during tasks, providing context beyond observable actions. In remote unmoderated testing, researchers cannot remind a quiet participant to continue speaking as they can in a moderated session. (high confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-moderated-usability-testing · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Moderated and unmoderated usability testing · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/remote-usability-tests/, https://www.nngroup.com/articles/usability-testing-101/
- [statement] Do not use a satisfaction score alone to diagnose an interface failure or assume that a favorable SUS score proves successful task performance. Combine ratings with observed performance and investigation of the problems. (medium confidence) — https://measuringu.com/sus/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX measurement, usability metrics and psychometric scales · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/measuring-perceived-usability/
- [statement] Use Goals–Signals–Metrics to make measurement actionable: articulate the product or feature goal, identify behavior or attitudes that signal success or failure, then define specific metrics. The official publication describes the framework as a way to connect product goals and metrics. (medium confidence) — https://research.google.com/pubs/archive/36299.pdf · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX measurement, usability metrics and psychometric scales · also: https://research.google/pubs/measuring-the-user-experience-on-a-large-scale-user-centered-metrics-for-web-applications/
- [statement] Small samples limit inference even when an instrument is reliable. Sauro recommends a confidence interval around the sample SUS score because small samples produce imprecise population estimates; Sauro and Dumas found low detection rates for post-task instruments at small sample sizes in their experiment. (medium confidence) — https://measuringu.com/sus/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX measurement, usability metrics and psychometric scales · also: https://measuringu.com/papers/Sauro_Dumas_CHI2009.pdf
- [statement] The Goals–Signals–Metrics process starts with a product or feature goal, identifies behavioral or attitudinal signals of success or failure, and translates them into metrics. Prefer signals specific to the goal, normalize raw counts when user-base growth would distort interpretation, and check logging coverage and automated traffic. (low confidence) — https://research.google.com/pubs/archive/36299.pdf · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX measurement, usability metrics and psychometric scales
- [statement] Scale research effort to the risk, consequences, and reversibility of the decision as well as research cost; expensive choices justify stronger triangulation than simple, easily reversible choices. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/triangulation-better-research-results-using-multiple-ux-methods/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX research strategy and method selection · also: https://enterprisearchitecture.harvard.edu/user-research-methods-and-recommendations
- [statement] Treat generated persona content as a representation requiring validation, not as observed human evidence: the conceptual analysis of generative personas describes convincing fabricated content as a hallucination risk, while NN/G requires persona characteristics to be grounded in real-user research. (medium confidence) — https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1071581925002149 · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX research synthesis, personas and jobs-to-be-done · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/persona/

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] Use open, neutral questions and short clarification probes; ask for concrete past episodes instead of inviting agreement with a proposed product or predicting future use. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-in-depth-interviews · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://entrepreneur.nyu.edu/blog/2026/03/28/stop-asking-what-they-want-why-customer-discovery-is-about-problems-not-products/
- [statement] Discovery interviews investigate users’ circumstances, problems, and existing ways of addressing them; use the conversation to understand their world rather than pitch a proposed product. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-in-depth-interviews · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://entrepreneur.nyu.edu/blog/2026/03/28/stop-asking-what-they-want-why-customer-discovery-is-about-problems-not-products/
- [statement] Use open, neutral starter questions and short probes for detail; ask participants to explain actions or clarify meaning rather than supply an expected answer. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-in-depth-interviews · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/
- [statement] Ground interviews in specific stories and real examples; asking about the last occurrence, what the person did, and what they previously tried keeps discovery focused on reported past behavior rather than hypothetical product adoption. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-in-depth-interviews · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://entrepreneur.nyu.edu/blog/2026/03/28/stop-asking-what-they-want-why-customer-discovery-is-about-problems-not-products/
- [statement] NN/G cautions that retrospective process accounts can omit important reasoning and habitual details, and recommends validating recollections with observation; a past-behavior account should therefore be treated as a report to investigate rather than guaranteed truth. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX
- [statement] NN/G advises using direct observation with later clarification when participants cannot safely be interrupted, and scopes contextual inquiry toward understanding complex work rather than assuming its interview component is always necessary. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX
- [statement] Treat lifecycle phases as revisitable activities rather than a one-way approval sequence: the Design Council says learning can return teams to earlier work, and van der Bijl-Brouwer’s public and social innovation study found nonlinear co-evolution of problem frames and solution spaces. (medium confidence) — https://www.designcouncil.org.uk/our-resources/the-double-diamond/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Human-centered design lifecycle and problem framing · also: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405872618301114
- [statement] In their survey of practitioners’ client innovation projects, Dell’Era and colleagues report that reframing practices were positively associated with innovation radicalness whereas framing practices were not. They explicitly state that their cross-sectional data limit causal inference over time; this is contextual evidence rather than proof that a lifecycle guarantees innovation. (low confidence) — https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0148296326002559 · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Human-centered design lifecycle and problem framing
- [statement] Human-centered design starts from understanding the people affected by a problem; IDEO U describes involving stakeholders throughout the process rather than only at its beginning or end. (medium confidence) — https://www.designcouncil.org.uk/our-resources/the-double-diamond/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Human-centered design lifecycle and problem framing · also: https://www.ideou.com/blogs/inspiration/what-is-human-centered-design?srsltid=AYCX9vKFS7wpqGtEIHQ-ADifYB5mUqj0FGMs5ntRc0yv06O8XicRYcJ8
- [statement] For assumptions, GOV.UK distinguishes hard constraints from processes that can change and uses constraints to prioritize risky assumptions for alpha. IDEO U likewise advises remaining receptive to being wrong rather than treating assumptions as settled knowledge. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/how-the-discovery-phase-works · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Human-centered design lifecycle and problem framing · also: https://www.ideou.com/blogs/inspiration/what-is-human-centered-design?srsltid=AYCX9vKFS7wpqGtEIHQ-ADifYB5mUqj0FGMs5ntRc0yv06O8XicRYcJ8
- [statement] Treat card-sort patterns as input to a draft taxonomy, then evaluate its labels and hierarchy through tree testing and revise problematic branches. Sorting results require design judgment rather than automatic adoption as the final structure. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/card-sorting-tree-testing-differences/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Information architecture, card sorting and tree testing · also: https://raw.studio/blog/card-sorting-and-tree-testing
- [statement] Use divergent navigation paths to consider cross-listing rather than forcing every item into one location. ONRR proposed cross-listing resources after participants split between plausible categories; NN/G recommends using observed demand rather than adding every theoretically possible placement. (medium confidence) — https://digital.gov/2022/01/06/open-source-information-architecture-design-using-the-tools-you-have-to-conduct-card-sorting-and-tree-testing · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Information architecture, card sorting and tree testing · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/interpreting-tree-test-results/
- [statement] Use representative content and clear card labels, and examine audience differences rather than assuming all users organize information alike. In the ONRR case, researchers selected cards using usage and search data, analyzed audiences separately, and found unclear labels impeded sorting. (low confidence) — https://digital.gov/2022/01/06/open-source-information-architecture-design-using-the-tools-you-have-to-conduct-card-sorting-and-tree-testing · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Information architecture, card sorting and tree testing
- [statement] Pilot card labels and avoid repeated wording that encourages superficial word matching instead of meaningful grouping. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/card-sorting-definition/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Information architecture, card sorting and tree testing
- [statement] Recruit actual or likely users of the service. Use screening questions about relevant circumstances or behavior rather than relying only on panel demographics. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-moderated-usability-testing · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Moderated and unmoderated usability testing · also: https://david-hamill.medium.com/unmoderated-usability-testing-some-mistakes-to-avoid-8f2d1a3d5732
- [statement] In its research on remote unmoderated think-aloud testing, MeasuringU reports a tradeoff: verbalizations can clarify behavior and aid problem discovery, while thinking aloud can increase task time and dropout. Its authors advise choosing according to the study objective rather than assuming think-aloud is always preferable. (low confidence) — https://measuringu.com/ta-summary-2023/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Moderated and unmoderated usability testing
- [statement] Remote testing can reach geographically dispersed users and show behavior on their own computers, while introducing technical troubleshooting demands; remote versus in-person location is a separate choice from whether a facilitator moderates the session. (high confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/remote-usability-tests/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Moderated and unmoderated usability testing · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/usability-testing-101/
- [statement] MeasuringU reports that its unmoderated think-aloud studies found benefits for problem discovery alongside increased dropout and longer task times, with task-level ease and confidence ratings also affected. Treat this as a method tradeoff in those studies, rather than assuming think-aloud leaves performance unchanged. (low confidence) — https://measuringu.com/ta-summary-2023/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Moderated and unmoderated usability testing
- [statement] Journey maps focus on customer actions, thoughts and feelings over time. Service blueprints connect customer actions to the organizational work that delivers the experience, rather than merely adding detail to the customer perspective. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/creating-an-experience-map · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Service design, journey mapping and service blueprints · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/service-blueprinting-faq/, https://www.smaply.com/blog/journey-map-vs-service-blueprint, https://www.nngroup.com/articles/service-blueprints-definition/
- [statement] Keep hypothetical current-state maps, research-based current-state maps and proposed future-state maps distinct; research-based maps should describe what actually happens rather than what stakeholders want to happen. (low confidence) — https://designnotes.blog.gov.uk/2016/04/21/how-to-make-a-user-journey-map/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Service design, journey mapping and service blueprints
- [statement] Do not treat invented workshop personas as human evidence: a published workshop case explicitly invented an end-user, whereas government guidance requires research-based maps to reflect real users rather than stakeholder assumptions. (medium confidence) — https://uxplanet.org/ux-case-study-customer-journey-service-blueprint-workshop-a0f7def0095 · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Service design, journey mapping and service blueprints · also: https://designnotes.blog.gov.uk/2016/04/21/how-to-make-a-user-journey-map/
- [statement] Use blueprint dependencies and cross-team handoffs to locate candidate failure points; a diagram identifies where to investigate and improve service delivery rather than establishing an improvement outcome by itself. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/service-blueprints-definition/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Service design, journey mapping and service blueprints · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6630975/, https://www.ijdesign.org/index.php/IJDesign/article/view/4911/1048
- [statement] Mapping terminology varies: Smaply confines journey maps to the customer side of the line of visibility, while government practitioners allow journey-map layers for departments, teams and supporting back-end systems. Specify the layers and purpose rather than relying on the artifact name alone. (low confidence) — https://www.smaply.com/blog/journey-map-vs-service-blueprint · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Service design, journey mapping and service blueprints · also: https://designnotes.blog.gov.uk/2016/04/21/how-to-make-a-user-journey-map/
- [statement] In blueprint terminology, evidence includes the props and places involved in service exchanges, such as physical stores, websites and emails; this layer can relate to both frontstage and backstage activity. This usage differs from research evidence used to substantiate a map. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/service-blueprints-definition/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Service design, journey mapping and service blueprints · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/service-blueprinting-faq/
- [statement] Scope a blueprint to a specific customer goal and scenario, align it with a business goal, and start with a focused problem. Smaply recommends expanding selected high-friction journey steps into operational layers instead of blueprinting every step by default. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/service-blueprints-definition/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Service design, journey mapping and service blueprints · also: https://www.smaply.com/blog/journey-map-vs-service-blueprint, https://www.nngroup.com/articles/service-blueprinting-faq/
- [statement] Ground current-experience maps in captured user experiences and research evidence instead of inventing customer actions or emotions. GOV.UK recommends event cards, relevant quotations, photos and research artefacts; Smaply likewise says maps and blueprints should be grounded in research rather than internal assumptions. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/creating-an-experience-map · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Service design, journey mapping and service blueprints · also: https://www.smaply.com/blog/journey-map-vs-service-blueprint
- [statement] Check the map against research and operational knowledge: review drafts with research observers and service-delivery teams, and involve knowledge holders from the blueprint phases and layers. For investigating failure points, Nielsen Norman Group recommends reviewing existing support tickets and other research, filling gaps, and combining attitudinal with behavioral evidence because reported behavior may differ from actual behavior. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/creating-an-experience-map · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Service design, journey mapping and service blueprints · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/service-blueprinting-faq/
- [statement] Measure task effectiveness with completion and errors, efficiency with completion time, and perceived usability with questionnaires; subjective ratings complement observed performance rather than replacing it. (medium confidence) — https://research.google.com/pubs/archive/36299.pdf · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX measurement, usability metrics and psychometric scales · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/measuring-perceived-usability/
- [statement] SUS is a ten-item, five-response-option questionnaire for perceived usability; administer it after the session to assess overall impressions rather than the difficulty of an individual task. (medium confidence) — https://measuringu.com/sus/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX measurement, usability metrics and psychometric scales · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/measuring-perceived-usability/
- [statement] A SUS score on its zero-to-one-hundred scale is not a percentage or a percentile. Interpret it against a relevant score distribution; norms describe relative standing rather than a universal usability pass mark. (medium confidence) — https://measuringu.com/sus/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX measurement, usability metrics and psychometric scales · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/measuring-perceived-usability/
- [statement] Keep reliability, validity, and precision separate: consistency of questionnaire responses differs from measuring the intended construct, and a small sample can still give an imprecise population estimate. MeasuringU recommends a confidence interval around the sample SUS score. (low confidence) — https://measuringu.com/sus/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX measurement, usability metrics and psychometric scales
- [statement] Google’s HEART framework groups metrics into Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention, and Task success. These are selectable categories rather than a requirement to track every category for every product. (low confidence) — https://research.google.com/pubs/archive/36299.pdf · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX measurement, usability metrics and psychometric scales
- [statement] MeasuringU says small SUS samples can retain reliable responses but yield imprecise population estimates and recommends confidence intervals. NN/g gives stricter practitioner advice against using numerical results from very small qualitative samples for design decisions. These positions warrant separating measurement reliability from inference precision rather than adopting a universal sample-size cutoff. (low confidence) — https://measuringu.com/sus/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX measurement, usability metrics and psychometric scales · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/measuring-perceived-usability/
- [statement] The often-cited average SUS score of 68 comes from Sauro’s historical set of 500 studies. Interpret it as a reference distribution, with percentile conversion as a separate operation, rather than treating the raw score as a percentage. (low confidence) — https://measuringu.com/sus/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX measurement, usability metrics and psychometric scales
- [statement] UMUX-Lite can be reported as separate item means, an aggregate, or a regression-based SUS-equivalent estimate. Label that conversion explicitly: the cited methodological account describes continued evaluation and refinement rather than establishing unconditional interchangeability with SUS. (low confidence) — https://measuringu.com/umux-lite/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX measurement, usability metrics and psychometric scales
- [statement] Analytics proxies need interpretation: Google’s paper notes that increased page views can indicate either popularity or confusion. Its authors recommend triangulating metrics with other research rather than allowing dashboard measures to stand alone. (low confidence) — https://research.google.com/pubs/archive/36299.pdf · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX measurement, usability metrics and psychometric scales
- [statement] Use generative research to explore needs and opportunities, and evaluative research to assess how well a proposed or existing solution meets user needs; these describe research purposes rather than a mandatory sequence of methods. (medium confidence) — https://www.userinterviews.com/ux-research-field-guide-chapter/how-to-choose-a-research-method · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX research strategy and method selection · also: https://enterprisearchitecture.harvard.edu/user-research-methods-and-recommendations, https://www.nngroup.com/articles/which-ux-research-methods/
- [statement] Synthetic-user output should be treated as model-generated hypotheses or supplementary material rather than observations from human participants; it cannot establish human experience without research with people. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/synthetic-users/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX research strategy and method selection · also: https://interactions.acm.org/archive/view/january-february-2026/the-challenges-of-synthetic-users-in-ux-research
- [statement] Treat method taxonomies as guides rather than rigid classifications: a method can collect more than one type of evidence or serve different objectives depending on the study design. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/which-ux-research-methods/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX research strategy and method selection
- [statement] When methods disagree, investigate study questions and conduct before choosing an interpretation. Check participant groups, tasks, logistics, and analysis; conflicting results can motivate further research rather than automatic preference for one data type. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/interpreting-research-findings/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX research strategy and method selection · also: https://dscout.com/people-nerds/triangulate-user-research
- [statement] Personas should synthesize research about real people rather than invent user evidence; the MOD case study explicitly excluded suspected personas that its research had not uncovered. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/persona/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX research synthesis, personas and jobs-to-be-done · also: https://defencedigital.blog.gov.uk/2021/05/17/understanding-online-working-in-defence-the-importance-of-personas-in-user-research/
- [statement] Klement criticizes attribute-based personas for failing to explain causality and proposes Job Stories; Laubheimer argues that behavioral personas and JTBD are compatible. These are attributed practitioner positions rather than proof of a universal replacement rule. (medium confidence) — https://www.intercom.com/blog/using-job-stories-design-features-ui-ux · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX research synthesis, personas and jobs-to-be-done · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/personas-jobs-be-done/
- [statement] When findings contradict a theme or each other, NN/G recommends checking participants, tasks, logistics and analysis before interpreting the difference; it recommends triangulating self-reported and observed evidence rather than following requests verbatim. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/interpreting-research-findings/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX research synthesis, personas and jobs-to-be-done
- [statement] Coding categorizes raw data. Inductive codes develop after reviewing data; deductive codes are defined before synthesis. Anderson describes goals, needs, motivations, tasks and pain points as useful categories in her workflow, rather than a mandatory taxonomy. (low confidence) — https://dscout.com/people-nerds/user-research-synthesis · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX research synthesis, personas and jobs-to-be-done
- [statement] Use personas as research-derived decision aids rather than replacements for research with people. NN/g explicitly cautions that persona-based expert reviews should not replace user testing. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/persona/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX research synthesis, personas and jobs-to-be-done

## Facts and statements

- [statement] Discovery interviews explore users’ circumstances, needs and problems; contextual inquiry combines interviewing with observation while people work in their usual environment. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-in-depth-interviews · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://dscout.com/people-nerds/behind-scenes-contextual-inquiry
- [statement] Keep discovery conversations centered on actual problems, actions and workarounds. Pitching a solution or asking whether someone would use it risks polite agreement being mistaken for evidence. (medium confidence) — https://entrepreneur.nyu.edu/blog/2026/03/28/stop-asking-what-they-want-why-customer-discovery-is-about-problems-not-products/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-in-depth-interviews
- [statement] Contextual inquiry combines observing real activities in the user’s normal environment with questions about how and why the work happens; contextual observation can expose effects of equipment, documents, and distractions. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/contextual-research-and-observation · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/
- [statement] Concrete examples still depend on memory: recalled accounts may lose details, and critical-incident interviews can emphasize extreme events while missing ordinary usage. Do not treat a detailed story as a complete record of behavior. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/critical-incident-technique/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://dscout.com/people-nerds/behind-scenes-contextual-inquiry
- [statement] Make the transition from conversation to observation explicit. Explain that the participant should continue normal work, how questions will interrupt it and that they may defer an interruption; otherwise they may stay in interview mode. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://dscout.com/people-nerds/behind-scenes-contextual-inquiry
- [statement] Record observed actions separately from interpretations, then ask participants to clarify what happened and correct your understanding. A wrap-up provides time to check interpretations without repeatedly interrupting the work. (medium confidence) — https://dscout.com/people-nerds/behind-scenes-contextual-inquiry · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/
- [statement] Obtain informed consent and explain the session before observation or interviewing; NN/G also calls for confidentiality discussion and approval for recording, while GOV.UK says to reconfirm consent before recording something new. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-in-depth-interviews · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/contextual-research-and-observation, https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/
- [statement] Actively seek contrary information and avoid communicating a preferred answer: prior beliefs can shape the interviewer’s interpretation, and participants may supply the answers they think the researcher wants. (medium confidence) — https://www.producttalk.org/glossary-discovery-confirmation-bias/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/
- [statement] NYU recommends looking for existing investments of time or money and workarounds as evidence of a problem; this is practitioner guidance for discovery, not a quantified predictive rule. (low confidence) — https://entrepreneur.nyu.edu/blog/2026/03/28/stop-asking-what-they-want-why-customer-discovery-is-about-problems-not-products/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX
- [statement] The Design Council names its Double Diamond activities Discover, Define, Develop and Deliver: understand the problem, use discovery insights to reframe it, explore alternative answers, and test small-scale solutions to reject or improve them. (low confidence) — https://www.designcouncil.org.uk/our-resources/the-double-diamond/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Human-centered design lifecycle and problem framing
- [statement] Frame an assigned solution as a problem before committing to it. Interrogate the brief, break down assumptions, and keep the initial problem statement open to revision through contact with people affected by it. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/how-the-discovery-phase-works · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Human-centered design lifecycle and problem framing · also: https://uxdesign.cc/how-to-properly-frame-your-design-challenge-eccb4d89cb83
- [statement] A useful framing exercise states the intended impact, records context and constraints, and revisits the question as understanding develops; scope also needs an explicit agreement about what falls outside the problem. (medium confidence) — https://uxdesign.cc/how-to-properly-frame-your-design-challenge-eccb4d89cb83 · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Human-centered design lifecycle and problem framing · also: https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/how-the-discovery-phase-works
- [statement] In GOV.UK’s delivery model, discovery ends with a decision whether to enter alpha. The decision considers whether a viable service would help users and whether pursuing it is cost effective; stopping after discovery can be the appropriate outcome. (low confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/how-the-discovery-phase-works · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Human-centered design lifecycle and problem framing
- [statement] GOV.UK recommends identifying hard and soft constraints during discovery. If work continues, dependencies that could make the service unviable should inform which risky assumptions receive attention during alpha. (low confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/how-the-discovery-phase-works · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Human-centered design lifecycle and problem framing
- [statement] GOV.UK’s transition to alpha calls for an understanding of the wider problem context, ideas to test and their initial priority, a rough team plan, and a plan for measuring success. These provide concrete readiness criteria for that transition. (low confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/how-the-discovery-phase-works · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Human-centered design lifecycle and problem framing
- [statement] Problem framing should allow alternatives to building the initially proposed service: GOV.UK explicitly lists content, campaigns, partnerships and better advice as possible responses, while Kal Joffres describes a project whose learning changed its initial app-education brief toward behaviour change. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/how-the-discovery-phase-works · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Human-centered design lifecycle and problem framing · also: https://marvelapp.com/blog/design-thinking-isnt-the-problem-human-centered-design/
- [statement] IDEO U presents Inspiration, Ideation and Implementation as overlapping phases; its account covers learning from people, translating insights into opportunities through early prototypes, and refining concepts with implementation planning. These are IDEO U’s phase labels. (low confidence) — https://www.ideou.com/blogs/inspiration/what-is-human-centered-design?srsltid=AYCX9vKFS7wpqGtEIHQ-ADifYB5mUqj0FGMs5ntRc0yv06O8XicRYcJ8 · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Human-centered design lifecycle and problem framing
- [statement] Treat the lifecycle as iterative: learning can change the problem frame and send a team back to earlier work. Design Council allows making and testing early ideas during discovery; IDEO U explicitly says its phases are not always linear. (medium confidence) — https://www.designcouncil.org.uk/our-resources/the-double-diamond/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Human-centered design lifecycle and problem framing · also: https://www.ideou.com/blogs/inspiration/what-is-human-centered-design?srsltid=AYCX9vKFS7wpqGtEIHQ-ADifYB5mUqj0FGMs5ntRc0yv06O8XicRYcJ8
- [statement] GOV.UK discovery guidance says to interrogate a prescribed solution, reframe it as a problem, break down assumptions and agree what falls outside the problem. Its example replaces a requirement to build an interactive map with the goal of helping people find their nearest contact centre. (low confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/how-the-discovery-phase-works · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Human-centered design lifecycle and problem framing
- [statement] GOV.UK discovery guidance cautions against starting to build the service during discovery and says research may identify alternatives to building a service at all. Scope that advice to service construction: Design Council separately allows early idea-making and testing within discovery. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/how-the-discovery-phase-works · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Human-centered design lifecycle and problem framing · also: https://www.designcouncil.org.uk/our-resources/the-double-diamond/
- [statement] Information architecture organizes content and labels to support finding information. Card sorting informs grouping and labeling decisions; it does not produce a complete navigation or search system. (medium confidence) — https://raw.studio/blog/card-sorting-and-tree-testing · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Information architecture, card sorting and tree testing · also: https://www.uxmatters.com/mt/archives/2007/09/card-sorting-mistakes-made-and-lessons-learned.php
- [statement] Card sorting asks participants to group content items, revealing candidate organizations; tree testing asks participants to find destinations within a proposed hierarchy, evaluating findability. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/card-sorting-tree-testing-differences/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Information architecture, card sorting and tree testing · also: https://raw.studio/blog/card-sorting-and-tree-testing, https://measuringu.com/tree-testing-ia/
- [statement] In an open card sort, participants create and name groups. In a closed sort, they assign cards to predefined categories. A hybrid sort supplies categories but permits participants to add their own. (medium confidence) — https://raw.studio/blog/card-sorting-and-tree-testing · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Information architecture, card sorting and tree testing · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/card-sorting-definition/
- [statement] NN/G cautions that predefined categories in a hybrid sort can bias participants toward similarly structured categories, and recommends considering that format only in specific circumstances. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/card-sorting-definition/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Information architecture, card sorting and tree testing
- [statement] Pilot card labels and avoid wording that invites superficial word matching. Ambiguous labels can prevent placement: the ONRR team reported this problem and planned to revise labels before its closed sort. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/card-sorting-definition/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Information architecture, card sorting and tree testing · also: https://digital.gov/2022/01/06/open-source-information-architecture-design-using-the-tools-you-have-to-conduct-card-sorting-and-tree-testing
- [statement] Analyze repeated groupings and labels, using similarity matrices to inspect co-grouping. Keep audience differences visible: ONRR normalized equivalent category names and examined its two user types separately. (medium confidence) — https://raw.studio/blog/card-sorting-and-tree-testing · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Information architecture, card sorting and tree testing · also: https://digital.gov/2022/01/06/open-source-information-architecture-design-using-the-tools-you-have-to-conduct-card-sorting-and-tree-testing
- [statement] Report success and path directness separately. Success concerns reaching the correct destination; directness concerns avoiding detours or backtracking. High eventual success can conceal difficult paths. (medium confidence) — https://raw.studio/blog/card-sorting-and-tree-testing · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Information architecture, card sorting and tree testing · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/interpreting-tree-test-results/
- [statement] Define acceptable destinations for each task before calculating tree-test success. Inspect failed destinations and paths as well as successful ones: NN/G notes that a participant can confidently choose a wrong destination without backtracking. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/interpreting-tree-test-results/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Information architecture, card sorting and tree testing
- [statement] Write realistic tree-test tasks without repeating category labels that give away the answer. Pilot the wording before the main study to detect ambiguity and priming. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/tree-testing/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Information architecture, card sorting and tree testing · also: https://digital.gov/2022/01/06/open-source-information-architecture-design-using-the-tools-you-have-to-conduct-card-sorting-and-tree-testing
- [statement] Small qualitative tree tests can explain confusing labels, while quantitative comparisons require larger samples and attention to uncertainty. NN/G recommends comparing alternative trees using the same tasks and considering confidence intervals and statistical significance. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/tree-testing/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Information architecture, card sorting and tree testing · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/interpreting-tree-test-results/
- [statement] A closed-card-sort resampling study found that estimated sample requirements depended on whether agreement was assessed through co-occurrence matrices or clustering similarity. Its authors identify a gender-skewed sample, a single tool and absent qualitative reasoning data as limitations; its findings should not be treated as a universal recruitment threshold. (low confidence) — https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3749012.3749050 · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Information architecture, card sorting and tree testing
- [statement] Do not expect a single broad card sort to solve findability. Sam Ng reports that mixing content granularity and market segments made earlier sorts difficult to manage; NN/G likewise says users may group the same content differently and final navigation decisions need judgment and additional research. (medium confidence) — https://www.uxmatters.com/mt/archives/2007/09/card-sorting-mistakes-made-and-lessons-learned.php · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Information architecture, card sorting and tree testing · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/card-sorting-tree-testing-differences/
- [statement] Interpret success together with directness and paths: eventual success may require backtracking, and a direct path can also end at a wrong destination. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/interpreting-tree-test-results/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Information architecture, card sorting and tree testing · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/tree-testing/
- [statement] Separate exploratory diagnosis from population estimates: a small qualitative tree test can reveal confusing labels, but quantitative success-rate estimates require a larger sample selected for the desired precision. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/tree-testing/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Information architecture, card sorting and tree testing · also: https://measuringu.com/tree-testing-ia/
- [statement] Moderated remote sessions involve real-time interaction between a facilitator and participant; in unmoderated remote testing participants complete predefined tasks independently on their own schedules and researchers review the resulting recordings or data later. (high confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/remote-usability-tests/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Moderated and unmoderated usability testing · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/usability-testing-101/, https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-moderated-usability-testing
- [statement] Write believable scenarios around participant goals and research questions. State the desired outcome without naming the interface actions or giving away the route to success. (high confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-moderated-usability-testing · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Moderated and unmoderated usability testing · also: https://userresearch.blog.gov.uk/2019/08/05/advice-for-better-moderated-usability-testing/, https://www.nngroup.com/articles/usability-testing-101/
- [statement] Moderators should introduce tasks neutrally and spend most of the session watching and listening. Prompts can interrupt or bias behavior, so avoid steering, correcting, or signaling agreement with participants. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-moderated-usability-testing · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Moderated and unmoderated usability testing · also: https://userresearch.blog.gov.uk/2019/08/05/advice-for-better-moderated-usability-testing/
- [statement] Small-sample guidance has a specific scope: NN/g recommends a small qualitative study of a single user group to find common problems, while Faulkner’s empirical resampling study demonstrates substantial variation in the problems found by equally sized small samples. These positions do not establish a universal guarantee of complete problem discovery. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/usability-testing-101/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Moderated and unmoderated usability testing · also: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/9032126_Beyond_the_five-user_assumption_Benefits_of_increased_sample_sizes_in_usability_testing
- [statement] Sourcegraph’s published usability-testing procedure specifies research questions, recruitment criteria, participant tasks, and task-success definitions before the study, to reduce scope creep and streamline analysis. (low confidence) — https://github.com/sourcegraph/handbook/blob/main/content/departments/product/design/research/usability-testing-how-to.md · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Moderated and unmoderated usability testing
- [statement] For reporting, Sourcegraph’s procedure records which participants succeeded or failed at each task and why they failed. Its findings template pairs task outcomes with suggested fixes and records additional observations about the overall experience. (low confidence) — https://github.com/sourcegraph/handbook/blob/main/content/departments/product/design/research/usability-testing-how-to.md · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Moderated and unmoderated usability testing
- [statement] Fan, Shi, and Truong’s industry survey identifies a tension between analysis speed and validity: reviewing think-aloud recordings takes time, and notes can be hard to match to their original context. Respondents describe better note-taking, shared observation, and discussion with peers as coping strategies. (low confidence) — https://www.mingmingfan.com/papers/JUS_Fan_Feb2020.pdf · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Moderated and unmoderated usability testing
- [statement] Usability testing observes actual or likely users attempting realistic tasks with a service or prototype to identify usability problems and improvements. (high confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-moderated-usability-testing · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Moderated and unmoderated usability testing · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/usability-testing-101/
- [statement] In moderated sessions, explain that the service is being tested, give neutral instructions, mainly watch and listen, and use follow-up questions to clarify observed behavior without steering the participant. (high confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-moderated-usability-testing · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Moderated and unmoderated usability testing · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/usability-testing-101/
- [statement] Nielsen Norman Group scopes its five-participant recommendation to a typical qualitative study of one user group, aimed at finding common problems. MeasuringU cautions that the guideline does not establish discovery of all problems and that sample-size assumptions depend on the same population, tasks, and application. (high confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/usability-testing-101/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Moderated and unmoderated usability testing · also: https://measuringu.com/five-history/
- [statement] Nielsen recommends quick debriefs and short findings reports for rapid design iterations, but detailed documentation of measurement methods for benchmark studies so later comparisons can reproduce the original study conditions. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/formal-vs-quick-usability-reports/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Moderated and unmoderated usability testing
- [statement] Service design organizes the people, resources and processes that deliver an experience; service blueprinting makes those delivery relationships visible for analysis and redesign. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/service-blueprints-definition/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Service design, journey mapping and service blueprints · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6630975/
- [statement] A blueprint links customer actions to frontstage actions visible to the customer, backstage actions performed out of view, and enabling support processes and systems. Frontstage interactions can involve staff or self-service technology. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/service-blueprints-definition/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Service design, journey mapping and service blueprints · also: https://www.smaply.com/blog/journey-map-vs-service-blueprint, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6630975/
- [statement] The line of interaction marks direct customer–organization interactions; the line of visibility separates visible frontstage activity from hidden backstage activity; the line of internal interaction separates contact work from deeper support functions. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/service-blueprints-definition/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Service design, journey mapping and service blueprints · also: https://www.smaply.com/blog/journey-map-vs-service-blueprint, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6630975/
- [statement] Blueprint evidence can mean physical or digital service cues such as signage, a website or an email inbox; this is distinct from the research observations, participant quotes and artefacts used to substantiate a map. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/service-blueprints-definition/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Service design, journey mapping and service blueprints · also: https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/creating-an-experience-map
- [statement] Scope a blueprint to a specific journey, user goal and improvement objective; different scenarios within the same service may require separate blueprints. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/service-blueprints-definition/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Service design, journey mapping and service blueprints
- [statement] Validate a draft map with research observers and teams who deliver the service, and involve frontline and support participants in examining blueprint steps for difficulties and problem areas. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/creating-an-experience-map · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Service design, journey mapping and service blueprints · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6630975/
- [statement] The digital-scribe case reports that blueprinting connected clinician actions and software processes for team communication, but its conclusions are exploratory and the project ended at conceptualization; it does not establish deployed service outcomes. (low confidence) — https://www.ijdesign.org/index.php/IJDesign/article/view/4911/1048 · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Service design, journey mapping and service blueprints
- [statement] Nielsen Norman Group defines service design as organizing people, props and processes to improve employee experience and, indirectly, customer experience; it identifies blueprinting as a service-design mapping tool. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/service-blueprints-definition/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Service design, journey mapping and service blueprints
- [statement] Nielsen Norman Group distinguishes current-state maps, which describe the existing experience, from future-state maps, which describe an ideal experience. It permits assumption-first hypothesis maps but warns that teams may stop before research validation and use hypotheses to make critical decisions; its hybrid approach follows the draft with user research and revision. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/journey-mapping-approaches/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Service design, journey mapping and service blueprints
- [statement] Treat journey maps and blueprints as maintained decision tools. Smaply warns that one-time deliverables go stale; GOV.UK recommends iteratively reviewing and revising draft maps until they accurately reflect user experience. (medium confidence) — https://www.smaply.com/blog/journey-map-vs-service-blueprint · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, Service design, journey mapping and service blueprints · also: https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/creating-an-experience-map
- [statement] Report which UMUX-LITE scoring convention and response scale you used. The original study adjusted the two-item score with regression to align with SUS; the practitioner guide also describes unadjusted item means and SUS-equivalent scores, so these outputs should not be silently interchanged. (medium confidence) — https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2470654.2481287 · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX measurement, usability metrics and psychometric scales · also: https://measuringu.com/umux-lite/
- [statement] Choose metrics whose interpretation follows the user goal. The HEART paper warns that more page views can reflect popularity or confusion, recommends normalizing counts as the user base grows, and calls for filtering automated traffic and checking instrumentation coverage. (low confidence) — https://research.google.com/pubs/archive/36299.pdf · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX measurement, usability metrics and psychometric scales
- [statement] The SEQ uses a seven-point easy–difficult rating immediately after a task. Comparisons across systems require comparable tasks; within a system it can identify relatively difficult task flows. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/measuring-perceived-usability/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX measurement, usability metrics and psychometric scales
- [statement] In their 2009 experiment, Sauro and Dumas found that the seven-point Likert task-difficulty question was easy to administer, correlated with other measures, and was as sensitive as their online mental-effort question. These findings concern the tasks and products studied. (low confidence) — https://measuringu.com/papers/Sauro_Dumas_CHI2009.pdf · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX measurement, usability metrics and psychometric scales
- [statement] Validity concerns whether an instrument measures its intended construct; reliability concerns response consistency; sensitivity concerns detecting meaningful differences. These are distinct from the precision of a population estimate. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/measuring-perceived-usability/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX measurement, usability metrics and psychometric scales · also: https://measuringu.com/sus/
- [statement] Start with the decision and the assumptions that need testing. Agree actionable research questions before choosing methods, and select activities that give reliable answers within the available time, effort, and cost. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/plan-user-research-for-your-service · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX research strategy and method selection · also: https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/plan-round-of-user-research
- [statement] Attitudinal research addresses reported beliefs and perceptions; behavioral research addresses actions. Select the evidence type that matches the question, and do not treat stated intentions as proof of future behavior. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/which-ux-research-methods/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX research strategy and method selection · also: https://www.userinterviews.com/ux-research-field-guide-chapter/how-to-choose-a-research-method
- [statement] Qualitative approaches are suited to exploring why or how a problem occurs and how it might be fixed; quantitative approaches are suited to questions about how many, how much, or how often. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/which-ux-research-methods/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX research strategy and method selection · also: https://www.userinterviews.com/ux-research-field-guide-chapter/how-to-choose-a-research-method, https://enterprisearchitecture.harvard.edu/user-research-methods-and-recommendations
- [statement] A research plan should identify questions and objectives, target user groups, research activities, recruitment, and the decisions each round will support; prepare the highest-priority rounds and revise the plan as learning develops. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/plan-user-research-for-your-service · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX research strategy and method selection · also: https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/plan-round-of-user-research
- [statement] Plan time for analysis and agree how findings will enter team decisions; collecting session data alone does not complete the research plan. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/plan-round-of-user-research · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX research strategy and method selection · also: https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/plan-user-research-for-your-service
- [statement] Triangulation combines complementary evidence or analytical perspectives on a question. Quantitative findings can indicate the extent of an issue while qualitative evidence helps explain it; evidence from one approach can guide a follow-up approach. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/triangulation-better-research-results-using-multiple-ux-methods/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX research strategy and method selection · also: https://maze.co/blog/mixed-methods-research/
- [statement] Using several methods does not automatically remove bias or resolve inconsistency: researchers must preserve methodological distinctions, check comparability, and address divergent interpretations. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9714985/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX research strategy and method selection · also: https://atlasti.com/guides/the-guide-to-mixed-methods-research/triangulation-in-mixed-methods-research
- [statement] Review existing evidence before commissioning new research: a decision may already be informed by available data, and triangulation can include existing analytics or customer-satisfaction information. (medium confidence) — https://www.userinterviews.com/ux-research-field-guide-chapter/how-to-choose-a-research-method · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods, UX research strategy and method selection · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/triangulation-better-research-results-using-multiple-ux-methods/
- [statement] Distinguish attitudinal evidence about what people say, think, or feel from behavioral evidence about what they do. Self-reported beliefs are limited by what participants know and are willing to report.
